schools.summary: Clarke lays out the crowded month (trumpets, tabernacles, the separation, this fast of confession); Wesley explains the grief comes only now, the festival joy past.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the sackcloth (Joel 1:8) and earth on the head (1 Sam. 4:12; 2 Sam. 1:2; Job 2:12); Ellicott: the external signs and the inner spirit were one.
Henry reads the fast God chose (Isa. 58:5-6) — a day to afflict the soul and loose the bands of wickedness, and above all a day of communion, for fasting without prayer is a body without a soul.
Gill anchors the date in the seventh month, Tisri, two days after the feast was ended.
Gill takes the separation of the putting away of heathen wives, a proof of the truth of their repentance.
Wesley and Clarke read it of the strange women again put away (cf. Ezra 10:3), whether new delinquents or old ones undiscovered, forsaking beloved sins.

Keil and Delitzsch deny it specially concerns the marriages — a voluntary renunciation of all heathen fellowship and customs; Ellicott hears deep propriety in 'seed,' the praise itself filled with confession.
Henry: a holy seed must separate from sin and sinners, for what communion hath light with darkness (2 Cor. 6:14).

debates.question: What was the separation 'from all strangers'?

sides.position: A putting away of the heathen wives, a resumed dissolution of mixed marriages proving their repentance
A voluntary renunciation of all fellowship with the heathen and of heathen customs, not specially the marriages

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch parse the two quarters — three hours reading, three confessing and worshipping (Neh. 8:7); Ellicott divides day and night into four, reading in the morning, worship in the afternoon.
Henry reckons six hours of solemn exercise, the word furnishing matter for prayer, but records Bishop Patrick's view that the whole twelve hours were spent in devotion.
Clarke gives Calmet's fuller scheme of four successive parts filling the day; Wesley keeps to three hours a quarter in a twelve-hour day.
Gill sets the people standing in the outer court to read and know the will of God.

debates.question: How was the day of reading and worship divided?

sides.position: Two quarters of the day — about three hours reading, three confessing and worshipping
The whole day in four successive parts, filled from morning to evening with reading, confession, and praise

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the Levites on the scaffold (Neh. 8:4), the two name-lists marking distinct acts; Ellicott ties it to Ezra's pulpit (Neh. 8:2), notes 'their God' vs 'your God,' and an uninserted prayer.
Henry: the ministers prayed successively (1 Cor. 14:31) or in eight congregations, and cried aloud not that God might hear like Baal's worshippers but to excite the people's fervency.
Wesley pictures several pulpits, each Levite teaching his portion, the loud voice testifying their deep sense of sin and importunate desire of mercy.
Gill sets them on an elevated place to be seen and heard by the people.
Keil and Delitzsch give the doxology summoning the people, the theme of the whole confession; Ellicott notes the singular 'thy glorious name' (Ps. 72:19) and the address gliding into adoration.
Clarke turns the summons 'stand up and bless' into a rebuke of congregations that sit while they profess to praise.
Henry: the name blessed is exalted above all blessing and praise — not the thousandth part is said of God's glory, for our goodness extendeth not to him.
Gill reads the roll of Levites who led the blessing.

outliers.note: Suggests the psalm was composed by Ezra though uttered by the Levites, noting the Septuagint omits the later names and inserts 'and Ezra said' before the doxology.

themes: stand up and bless the LORD
the glorious name above all praise
the doxology that opens the prayer

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch expound Jahve alone as Creator — 'heaven of heavens' (Deut. 10:14; 1 Kings 8:27), the sea (Ps. 146:6), the host (Gen. 2:1); Ellicott: the upholding reproduced only in Heb. 1:3, the host here angels (Ps. 103:21).
Clarke renders 'thou givest life to them all,' toys with Kepler's living heavens, then settles that 'preserve in being' need not imply vitality.
Henry adores God as the only living and true God, Creator, Protector, and object of the creatures' praise, exalted above all blessing.
Gill fixes the incommunicable name — Jehovah alone, the one only true and living God.

outliers.note: Muses on Kepler's notion that the heavenly host are instinct with life, before allowing that 'preserve in being' is a good meaning that need not imply vitality.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the recital — God chose Abram, brought him from Ur, gave him the name Abraham — as the opening of the long history of grace.
Clarke points for the calling and the new name to Exodus 13:21 and Genesis 17:5, where Abram becomes father of a multitude.
Henry: a distinguishing favour and a powerful grace that plucked one man from Chaldean idolatry — 'look unto Abraham your father' (Isa. 51:2).
Gill marks the sovereignty of the choice, from among the Chaldeans and out of his father's family.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the covenant to give the land of the six nations, performed because God is righteous (cf. Deut. 32:4; Neh. 9:33); Ellicott notes the Hivites are omitted from the list.
Henry: the covenant was sure, God finding Abraham's heart faithful because he made it so — faith being God's gift — and performing his words, upright with the upright (Ps. 18:25).
Gill glosses the faithful heart of a true believer, proved when he offered up his son (Gen. 22:2).

themes: a faithful heart, God's own gift
the covenant to give the land
God performs because he is righteous

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch unfold the two things compressed here — the affliction God saw (Exod. 3:7) and the cry at the Red Sea (Exod. 14:10) — answered by plagues and the parted waters.
Gill: God was no mere spectator of the bondage but looked on it with pity and sent a deliverer.
Henry: seasonable to recall the exodus while pleading for deliverance from Babylon — God saw the affliction and heard the cry.
Keil and Delitzsch (leaning on Deut. 6:22): the signs were wrought because the Egyptians dealt proudly, and God made himself a name, as this day.
Gill takes the signs and wonders of the ten plagues inflicted on Pharaoh and his people.
Henry: where they dealt proudly God showed himself above them (Exod. 18:11) and got himself a name (Exod. 14:17), glorified to this day.
Keil and Delitzsch frame the crying answered by the parted sea and the pursuers cast in; Ellicott bids compare the Song of Moses (Exod. 15:5), marking identity and variation in the Hebrew.
Henry: one act both saved and destroyed — the people led through, the persecutors thrown into the deeps as a stone into mighty waters.
Gill reads the plain wonder of a path opened through the midst of the sea on dry land.

themes: echo of the Song of Moses
salvation and destruction in one act

schools.summary: Clarke distinguishes the cloud's three offices — a pillar guiding by day, a fire lighting and rallying by night, an extended cloud refreshing with dew and shade.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain office of the cloud and fire leading them in the way, the next stage of the recital.
Henry: the pillar directed all their stages and steps, and was named again (Neh. 9:19) as a forfeited mercy still continued — cause for double thankfulness.
Gill reads the day-pillar as a shelter from the sun in a barren wilderness.

themes: the pillar of cloud and fire

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the recital of God coming down and giving right judgments and true laws; Ellicott hears five names of the law from Psalm 119, the emphasis on 'right, true, good' as the Decalogue's eternal principles.
Wesley: the moral and judicial precepts founded on natural equity, the ceremonial statutes tokens of goodness and types of gospel grace.
Henry: the greatest favour of all — the Lawgiver glorious in coming down (Deut. 4:33), no nation with such laws (Deut. 4:8), the ceremonies types of gospel grace.
Gill guards the condescension of the descent, consistent with God's omnipresence.

themes: the goodness of the whole law

schools.summary: Ellicott bids note every word and the prominence of the sabbath, foreshadowing its weight in the sworn covenant (Neh. 10:31).
Clarke hears in 'madest known' a hint they had forgotten the ordinance during their sojourn in Egypt.
Henry: a token of special favour distinguishing them from the revolted nations and a means of communion, given with the law and the good Spirit.
Gill: a rest corporeal and spiritual, peculiar to the nation and typical of the rest in Christ.

themes: forgotten in Egypt, revealed at Sinai

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the three gifts together — bread, water, the sworn land; Ellicott: 'bread from heaven' a phrase our Lord consecrated for ever (John 6:32).
Henry: meat and drink for the way and the good land at the journey's end — what would they more? — a provision repeated through forty years.
Gill reads the bread from heaven of the manna given to satisfy their hunger.

themes: supply for the way and the rest

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the emphatic 'they, even our fathers,' the hardened neck glancing back to the calf (Exod. 32:9; 33:3); Ellicott: 'dealt proudly,' the same word used of the Egyptians (Exod. 18:11).
Henry: pride is at the bottom of disobedience — they heard the word but hearkened not, saw the works but were not mindful of the wonders as miracles or as mercies.
Gill: they behaved haughtily toward God their kind benefactor.

Keil and Delitzsch gather the refusal against the great confession of a God ready to pardon; Ellicott prefers the reading 'in Egypt' and notes 'a God of pardons' occurs only here, Dan. 9:9, and Ps. 130:4.
Clarke judges 'in their rebellion' an error for 'in Egypt' (MSS, LXX, Num. 14:4); Wesley reads 'made' as 'designed,' as Abraham is said to have offered Isaac (Heb. 11:17).
Henry names the two sins — the meditated return to slavery and the calf — yet crowns them with the pardon, a God forgiving iniquity (Exod. 34:6).
Gill: sheer obstinacy — though exhorted and threatened, they refused to obey.

debates.question: Did the fathers actually appoint a captain to return to Egypt, or only resolve to?

sides.position: An accomplished act of rebellion — they set up a captain to return
Only designed or resolved, never carried out, as the proposal of Numbers 14:4

themes: a captain to return to bondage

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the emphatic 'yea, they even made a molten calf,' the blasphemous ascription of the exodus to an image, and the refrain of 'great provocations.'
Gill: a calf in imitation of the Apis, the sacred ox of the Egyptians.
Henry: the second great sin — Egyptian idolatry, so sottish as to say 'This is thy God,' changing their glory into the likeness of an ox (Ps. 106:20).

themes: the darkest sin before the greatest mercy

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the continued gifts — the pillar not departing, the good Spirit, manna, water — as grace outlasting the calf; Clarke sharpens 'from over them' and recalls the cloud's three offices.
Henry: the pillar named again on purpose — though they provoked God to withdraw, he took it not away (Neh. 9:12); forfeited mercies continued call for double thankfulness.
Gill: God forsook them not where no supply could be had, and to be forsaken was to be lost.
Ellicott ties the good Spirit to the elders (Num. 11:17, 25) and Psalm 143:10, marking the teaching Spirit as here only, a striking anticipation of the New Testament.
Gill takes the good Spirit of the spirit of prophecy, and, with Aben Ezra, of the Spirit put upon the seventy elders (Num. 11:17).
Henry sets the instructing Spirit beside the law and the books of Moses, seen in Bezaleel (Exod. 31:3), Joshua (Num. 27:18), and Caleb (Num. 14:24).

themes: the inward gift with the outward
an anticipation of the New Testament

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the summation of the wilderness mercies — sustained forty years, lacking nothing, clothes not worn, feet not swollen.
Clarke fixes on the clothes that waxed not old, pointing to the parallel of Deuteronomy 8:4.
Henry: never a people so long and tenderly nursed, carried as upon eagles' wings (Deut. 32:11).
Gill: they wanted neither for food nor raiment through forty years.

Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott read the trans-Jordan conquests of Sihon and Og as the earnest of Canaan, taking 'divide into corners' of the land portioned by boundaries, with a double reference to the one Sihon of Heshbon.
Clarke presses the textual difficulty that Sihon was king of Heshbon, so one land is meant, not two; Wesley reads 'corners' of the heathen driven and cooped into corners while Israel dwelt at large.
Gill: the two kingdoms of Sihon and Og and the seven nations of Canaan.

debates.question: What does 'thou didst divide them into corners' mean?

sides.position: The heathen nations were destroyed and their remnants cooped up into corners of the land
God divided the conquered land unto Israel by its boundaries

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch join the increase to the entrance — multiplied as the stars and brought into the promised land, two halves of one kept word.
Gill: the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham, six hundred thousand men besides women and children (cf. Gen. 15:5).
Henry: made numerous to replenish the land and victorious to master it — the oath of the stars made good (Gen. 22:17; Deut. 10:22).
Keil and Delitzsch: the children went in and possessed it, God subduing the Canaanites and giving them with their kings into Israel's hands.
Gill notes the word 'children' — not the fathers, who died in the wilderness (Num. 14:29), but their children inherited the promise.
Henry: the conquest was pure gift, the natives given up and the necks of kings under their feet (Josh. 10:24).

themes: the fathers' unbelief shut them out

schools.summary: Gill: strong cities said to be walled up to heaven (Deut. 1:28), a fat land and houses full of good things found ready to hand.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the catalogue — cities, fat land, full houses — culminating in delight in God's great goodness, the summit before the fall.
Clarke reads a warning in the fatness — they grew effeminate and luxurious and corrupt, then were destroyed, a law of nations he backs from a Roman historian.

outliers.note: Turns Israel's fatness into a general law of nations — war begets poverty, peace affluence, affluence luxury and corruption — citing a Roman historian.

themes: strong cities and a fat land

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: a general condemnation — they cast God's law behind their backs (1 Kings 14:9; Ezek. 23:35) and slew the prophets (2 Chron. 24:21; 1 Kings 19:10) who testified against them (2 Kings 17:13).
Gill: great ingratitude — after all these mercies they were disobedient and rebelled.
Henry: they slew the prophets who testified to turn them to God, returning the greatest injury for the greatest kindness (cf. Matt. 23:37).

themes: the law cast behind their backs

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch refer the verse to the judges (Judg. 2:11), the 'saviours' being the judges (Judg. 3:9), the cycle turning many times; Ellicott: the phraseology shows the Book of Judges remembered.
Clarke: the whole book of Judges is a history of God's mercies and their rebellions.
Henry: upon their humble request God gave them saviours, not for merit but according to his manifold mercies.
Gill names the oppressors — kings of Mesopotamia, Moab, Canaan — into whose hand a rebellious people was given.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the revolving pattern — rest, evil again, the enemy's hand, the cry, deliverance according to God's mercies, many times over.
Gill: in the ease of rest and prosperity they did evil again.
Henry: they were wrought upon neither by trouble nor by deliverance — neither fear nor love would hold them to their duty (Judg. 3:12; 4:1).

themes: the turning wheel of sin and rescue
neither fear nor love held them
mercy that still met the cry

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the law is the way of life (Lev. 18:5; Ezek. 20:11), but they gave a resisting shoulder (Zech. 7:11) like an ox rearing against the yoke (Hos. 4:16).
Gill: God testified against them by sending prophets to admonish and remind them of their duty.
Henry: refusing to do what would make them live, they forsook their own mercies — a withdrawing shoulder, the law not of faith (Gal. 3:12).

themes: which if a man do he shall live

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'thou didst draw out' favour (Jer. 31:3) across the kingly rule from Solomon to the Assyrians, the giving up to the peoples (Ps. 106:41) beginning with Assyria.
Clarke reckons some 254 years of forbearance with the ten tribes, and finds in 'by thy Spirit in thy prophets' the true notion of divine inspiration.
Henry: God forbore many years, loath to punish; the prophets' testimony was the Spirit of Christ in them (1 Pet. 1:11), sent in compassion lest he send judgments (2 Chron. 36:15).
Gill: longsuffering through many reigns — 'thou didst draw out' mercy from God's very heart.

outliers.note: Reads 'by thy Spirit in thy prophets' as the true notion of divine inspiration — the Spirit given to the prophets, who testify as they are moved.

themes: given at last to the peoples

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch ground the sparing in God's promise not to make a full end (Jer. 4:27; 30:11) — a remnant preserved and delivered from exile.
Gill: for the displaying of his great and abundant mercy they were not consumed.
Henry: he did not stir up all his wrath, designing their reformation and not their destruction.

themes: mercy as the ground of survival

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: may the covenant-keeping God now look on the affliction of his bondmen; Ellicott marks the prayer proper beginning, the kings of Assyria the rod of God's anger (Isa. 10:5).
Clarke reads the whole frame of society in the roll of sufferers; Wesley: 'mercy' is added because the broken covenant is no sufficient ground of hope, so they fly to God's free mercy.

Henry: the one petition of the prayer — that the universal, long-borne trouble not seem little — pleading God as feared (Deut. 7:21) and trusted (Dan. 9:4), who came down when he saw Egypt's affliction (Exod. 3:7).
Gill notes the divine titles are Nehemiah's own, so the prayer is likely his composure.

themes: let not the trouble seem little

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: God is just concerning all, only fulfilling his word upon sinners (Deut. 32:4; Ezra 9:15); the prophets are omitted next as his witnesses.
Wesley: under the sharpest rebukes we must still justify God and own we are punished less than our iniquities deserve.
Henry: they justify God and judge themselves — he will be clear when he judgeth (Ps. 51:4).
Gill: they could complain of no wrong, and unmixed judgment would have been but their desert.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott note the prophets are deliberately omitted from the roll of the guilty, as God's witnesses, though they shared the suffering.
Clarke: kings, princes, priests, and fathers broke the law, but the prophets remained faithful, testifying by the Spirit even at the risk of their lives.
Gill: all ranks, from highest to lowest, showed no obedience to the holy law.
Keil and Delitzsch take 'in their kingdom' of the independent realm, amid the great goodness and the wide land (Exod. 3:8), yet they turned not from their wicked works.
Clarke prefers the reading 'in thy kingdom' (MSS, LXX, Syriac, Arabic), that all their dominion was in truth the LORD's.
Henry: a contempt of the good land — those who would not serve God in their own land were made to serve enemies in a strange one (Deut. 28:47; 32:15).
Gill: they served not God even in their most flourishing circumstances, of Israel or of Judah.

debates.question: Should the text read 'in their kingdom' or 'in thy kingdom'?

sides.position: 'In their kingdom' — the independent realm God had given them
'In thy kingdom' — the reading of manuscripts and versions, that all their dominion was the LORD's

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch support the petition by the present state — bondmen of the Persian kings in the land God gave the fathers as a free people, its increase belonging to their rulers.
Gill: leave to return, yet still in subjection to the kings of Persia in the land God gave.
Clarke: no king of their own, under Persia, paying a regular tribute.
Henry: free-born Israelites enslaved, holding by base tenure the land once given by the crown of heaven — poverty and slavery the fruits of sin (cf. Ezra 9:9).

themes: bondmen in the land of the fathers

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch complete the plea — the increase belongs to the kings, who rule bodies and cattle at their pleasure; Ellicott adds the tribute sent to Persia and hears in the distress a grief at remembering God's judgments.
Clarke: personal and feudal services exacted at the ruler's pleasure, nothing their own; Wesley: they labour and God blesses, yet the increase goes to the kings in heavy tribute.
Gill: a fruitful land, yet its profit lessened by the toll, tribute, and custom of foreign kings.

debates.question: Where does the sting of 'great distress' chiefly lie?

sides.position: In the outward Persian oppression — tribute and forced service draining a fruitful land
Less in the Persian yoke than in the grief of remembering God's judgments upon a covenant people

schools.summary: Ellicott: on the ground of the confession they make a sure covenant and seal it, each impressing his seal on hardened clay or by a string (cf. Neh. 11:1).

Clarke reads the signatories as a mixed government, nobles civil and priests ecclesiastical, each supporting the other (Matt. 22:21); Wesley: sealed and left on record as a witness against them if they dealt deceitfully.
Henry: a sure covenant made with serious consideration, solemnity, joint consent, and fixed resolution, fulfilling the perpetual covenant (Jer. 50:5) and the subscribing hand (Isa. 44:5).
Gill: 'because of all this,' or 'in the midst of all this evil,' they bind themselves anew to God.

themes: a sure covenant made and sealed
the confession issues in a bond
